relations.note: The Younger Avesta repeatedly calls Atar the son of Ahura Mazda.

relations.myth: Mazda's fire reveals and executes moral judgment
relations.note: Atar is Mazda's mighty fire, aiding truth and judging truth against deceit.
relations.date: late second or early first millennium BCE

relations.myth: Ohrmazd creates fire within the material creation
relations.note: Later creation doctrine treats fire as a spiritual and material creation of Ohrmazd.

relations.myth: Fire complains to Ohrmazd about pollution
relations.note: Fire complains that material existence exposes it to contamination; Ohrmazd explains its worldly role.
relations.source: Dēnkard summary of a lost Avestan nask

relations.note: Atar and Asha Vahishta join the good host contesting the Glory.
Later theology assigns fire to Asha Vahishta as its guardian and material creation.
Spenta Mainyu leads the good host, including Atar, against the evil host.

relations.myth: Mazda distributes good through spirit and fire
relations.note: Mazda distributes good to the opposing moral parties through Spenta Mainyu and fire.
relations.date: late second or early first millennium BCE

relations.note: Vohu Manah and Atar belong to the good company casting darts for the Glory.
Angra Mainyu leads the evil host opposing Atar's company over the Glory.

relations.myth: Ahriman's invasion introduces smoke into fire
relations.note: Ahriman afflicts originally pure fire with smoke during his assault on creation.
Akem Manah joins the evil host opposing Atar and the good divinities.
Aeshma joins the evil host opposing Atar's company in the contest.

relations.myth: Atar and Aži Dahāka contest the Glory
relations.note: They threaten to extinguish or burn one another; both retreat without gaining the Glory.
Spityura appears among the evil host opposing Atar, without individual combat.

relations.myth: The Glory escapes into Lake Vourukaša
relations.note: Apąm Napāt takes the Glory after Atar and Aži Dahāka frighten one another away.
At the Renovation, Fire and Airyaman melt the mountains' metals into a purifying river.
Atar's molten-metal purification occurs during the Renovation brought about by the final Saoshyant.
The epithet victorious fire was secondarily reinterpreted as Fire of Bahrām, without an Avestan encounter.
relations.source: Middle Persian development of ātar vərəθraγan

relations.note: Ādur Burzēn-Mihr bears Mihr's name, probably through a human founder; no divine encounter survives.
Fire and water-goddess sanctuaries occupied the same royal complex, without a surviving mythic meeting.
